root_packet.account: The complete solution set is ten triples: (3,7,42), (3,8,24), (3,9,18), (3,10,15), (3,12,12), (4,5,20), (4,6,12), (4,8,8), (5,5,10), (6,6,6). The three children agree with no mathematical conflict, and the audit independently re-derived the bounds, the factoring bijection, and every substitution check. Proof structure for the final document: (i) Bounds. Since 1/y+1/z > 0, x=1 gives 1/x = 1 > 1/2 and x=2 gives 1/x = 1/2, each forcing the total above 1/2, so x >= 3; and x <= y <= z gives 1/2 = 1/x+1/y+1/z <= 3/x, so x <= 6. Hence x in {3,4,5,6} (root.03-independent-audit:C002). (ii) Per-case bijection. For fixed x, clearing 1/y+1/z = (x-2)/(2x) gives ((x-2)y-2x)((x-2)z-2x) = 4x^2, a bijection between solutions with x <= y <= z and positive factor pairs A <= B of 4x^2 satisfying the integrality congruence and the y >= x filter (audit:C003); equivalently the reduced per-case forms: x=3: (y-6)(z-6)=36 with y,z > 6; x=4: (y-4)(z-4)=16 with y,z > 4; x=5: (3y-10)(3z-10)=100 requiring both factors congruent to 2 mod 3; x=6: (y-3)(z-3)=9. Each right-hand side has finitely many divisor pairs, so full enumeration is a complete case analysis. (iii) Enumerations. 36: pairs (1,36),(2,18),(3,12),(4,9),(6,6) yield five triples (case-x3-x4:C002). 16: pairs (1,16),(2,8),(4,4) yield three (case-x3-x4:C005). 100: of the five pairs (1,100),(2,50),(4,25),(5,20),(10,10), only (2,50) and (5,20) are congruent to 2 mod 3 in both entries; (2,50) gives y=4 < 5 and is rejected; (5,20) gives (5,5,10) (case-x5-x6:C003,C004,C005). 9: (1,9) gives y=4 < 6, rejected; (3,3) gives (6,6,6) (case-x5-x6:C006). (iv) Verification. Each of the ten triples is confirmed by exact common-denominator substitution, done once by the case children and again independently by the audit; all ten pass. (v) Count. The audit objective's phrase 'nine candidate triples' mislabels the ten-element list it itself enumerates; the case tallies 5+3+1+1 = 10 resolve the mismatch in favor of ten. The sibling-coverage gaps flagged by each case child are closed at this node because all four x-slices are now joined. All methods are bounds, factorization, and divisor enumeration in exact integer arithmetic, satisfying D1-D4.

claims.statement: For each fixed x in {3,4,5,6}, clearing denominators in 1/y+1/z = (x-2)/(2x) yields the product equation ((x-2)y-2x)((x-2)z-2x) = 4x^2, a bijection between solutions (y,z) with x <= y <= z and positive factor pairs A <= B of 4x^2 meeting the integrality congruence and the size filter (A+2x)/(x-2) >= x; since 4x^2 has finitely many divisor pairs, enumerating all of them is a complete case analysis.

Case x=3: the equation is (y-6)(z-6) = 36 with y,z > 6; the ordered divisor pairs (1,36),(2,18),(3,12),(4,9),(6,6) of 36 give exactly the five triples (3,7,42), (3,8,24), (3,9,18), (3,10,15), (3,12,12), and no others.
Case x=4: the equation is (y-4)(z-4) = 16 with y,z > 4; the ordered divisor pairs (1,16),(2,8),(4,4) of 16 give exactly the three triples (4,5,20), (4,6,12), (4,8,8), and no others.

Case x=5: the equation is (3y-10)(3z-10) = 100, and integer y,z require both factors congruent to 2 mod 3; of the five ordered pairs (1,100),(2,50),(4,25),(5,20),(10,10) only (2,50) and (5,20) qualify, (2,50) gives y=4 < x=5 and is rejected by the ordering, and (5,20) gives the unique triple (5,5,10).
